case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbourline Ferries (HLF) is a private limited company in the coastal ferry and tourism transport sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 1998 by Eamon Doyle, it operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. HLF plans to invest $560,000 in a hybrid-electric ferry and online booking system, financed by a $320,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $220,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and produces 60,000 units a year. HLF faces a 4.6% passenger complaint rate and rising crew absenteeism. Eamon Doyle approves every timetable change himself, and all sailings still use the old port terminal.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: HLF sold 60,000 passenger trips last year, up 5% on the previous year, but 4.6% of passengers complained and 26 written complaints were logged last month. Only 89% of sailings left on time, against a 95% target, and average berth turnaround was 42 minutes. A survey of 420 tourists found 70% would pay $1.20 more for a guaranteed-seat premium service, and 55% book by price. Thirteen of the 48 crew need hybrid-engine training at $950 each. The ticket refund rate is 3.4%.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harbourline Ferries (HLF) for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate has risen from 4.4% to 5.1%, increasing the cost of variable-rate business borrowing. (2) Marine fuel and electricity input prices have risen 2.1% year-on-year. (3) Consumer spending on coastal day trips fell 8.5% in the latest quarter, while spending on city breaks rose 2.7%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for HLF of funding the $560,000 hybrid ferry from retained profit rather than the $320,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment, so HLF keeps cash to run 60,000 passenger trips a year. The base rate has risen from 4.4% to 5.1%, making the $320,000 five-year bank loan more costly, while the $240,000 retained profit is free. Each trip earns $5.50 ($13.50 − $8.00), or $330,000 at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 8.5% fall in coastal day-trip spending without raising the $13.50 fare.

Point 2: Funding from internal reserves avoids collateral and repossession risk on the $560,000 ferry if the 4.6% complaint rate delays the return from the new vessel. No lender can impose terms on Eamon Doyle's timetable decisions, which suits his direct control, and HLF keeps bank headroom for later booking-system upgrades. The retained profit also signals that the existing service generates enough surplus to support expansion without diluting ownership. The 5% growth in trips recorded in Appendix 1 makes that reserve useful if the new ferry needs early adjustment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Harbourline Ferries (HLF), its ferry investment and its cost structure.

questions.question_text: Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or partnerships with coastal hotels and tour operators. Which should HLF choose to promote its premium ferry service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A television campaign would show the hybrid ferry to a wide audience and build awareness of coastal travel. However, airtime is expensive for a 48-employee firm funding a $560,000 vessel, and most viewers live far from the route, so the spend would reach few of the 420 tourists in the survey.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and can target listeners near the port, which suits a time-sensitive message about sailings. Yet radio does not reach tourists planning a trip in advance, and the 89% on-time record needs a credibility message rather than a short jingle; coverage is too narrow to fill 60,000 trips against $220,000 of fixed costs.

Partnerships with coastal hotels and tour operators: Hotel and tour partnerships put HLF's premium offer in front of visitors already near the port, matching the 70% who would pay $1.20 more for a guaranteed seat. Partners can bundle tickets with stays, address the 55% who book on price with a package deal, and cost far less than television. The drawback is dependence on partners' willingness and slower reach than a media campaign.

Recommendation: HLF should choose partnerships with coastal hotels and tour operators. They reach the surveyed tourists, support the $1.20 premium and fit a $320,000 loan budget. National television is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful; local radio is rejected as too short-term. HLF should improve the 89% punctuality before promoting a guaranteed-seat product. HLF can measure bookings against the 420-tourist survey before renewing the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to HLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HLF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of HLF with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for HLF of using autocratic leadership when introducing the hybrid-electric ferry.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives clear, unambiguous instructions on new safety and engine routines, which matters when 13 of the 48 crew need hybrid-engine training at $950 each. With Eamon Doyle approving every timetable himself, decisions are fast and staff know exactly what is required, helping cut the 4.6% complaint rate and improve the 89% on-time sailing record during the technology change.

Point 2: Central decisions stop conflicting practices between crews and keep berth turnaround near the stated 42 minutes, protecting the 60,000-trip plan and the $5.50 contribution ($13.50 − $8.00). Firm direction can also enforce attendance while crew absenteeism rises, and the 26 written complaints can be addressed through one consistent service standard. The risk is lower staff ownership, so HLF should explain the reasons for decisions to maintain morale. The 5% rise in trips recorded in Appendix 1 makes that clarity valuable as the new ferry beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis linked to HLF's ferry introduction, complaints and punctuality.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job familiarisation for the 13 crew or funded hybrid-engine training at $950 each. Which should HLF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job familiarisation: Crew learn the hybrid ferry on the route they will actually sail, with no course fee and no time away from the 60,000-trip schedule. It fits Eamon Doyle's direct instructions and can quickly address the 42-minute berth turnaround. However, it cannot cover the technical safety knowledge needed for a new engine, may pass on old habits, and gives no certificate to reassure tourists.

Funded hybrid-engine training: The $950 course gives the 13 crew formal competence on the new system, directly reducing the risk behind the 4.6% complaint rate and supporting the guaranteed-seat offer that 70% of surveyed tourists value. Thirteen places cost $12,350 (13 × $950), a known sum against the $560,000 ferry. The drawback is time off the boat, which could worsen the 89% punctuality record and the 26 complaints while training runs.

Decision: HLF should fund the hybrid-engine training for the 13 crew, with short on-board familiarisation afterwards. Formal competence is essential on a new vessel and the cost is explicit at $12,350, whereas on-the-job familiarisation alone is rejected because it cannot provide the technical qualification and may embed unsafe routines. HLF should stagger the courses so that sailings continue. A further consideration is the 8.5% fall in coastal day-trip spending: with demand weak, spending on qualification must earn its keep through fewer complaints and refunds. Eamon Doyle can schedule the training in the quieter period before peak sailings, keeping the 60,000-trip plan intact. HLF should check the 4.6% complaint rate after the courses before funding places for any further crew.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to HLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of HLF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the insert figures.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HLF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $220,000 ÷ ($13.50 − $8.00) = $220,000 ÷ $5.50 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 passenger trips a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.50 − $8.00 = $5.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HLF's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 40,000-trip break-even with 60,000 trips sold: the margin of safety is 20,000 trips, a buffer if the 8.5% fall in coastal day-trip spending reduces bookings.
2. Use the $5.50 contribution to test the $1.20 premium wanted by 70% of surveyed tourists: the $13.50 fare can be modelled with the $8.00 variable cost held constant.
3. Check that 60,000 × $5.50 = $330,000 of contribution covers $220,000 of fixed costs and can service the $320,000 loan as the base rate reaches 5.1%.
4. Benchmark average total cost of about $11.67 a trip ($220,000 ÷ 60,000 + $8.00) against the 3.4% refund rate and crew absenteeism to judge whether the new ferry is used efficiently.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 20,000-trip margin of safety under weak tourism spending; $1.20 premium modelling on $13.50 and $8.00; $330,000 contribution to cover $220,000 fixed costs and the $320,000 loan; unit-cost benchmarking at $11.67 to tackle refunds and absenteeism.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HLF's profitability between 2024 and 2025. Has profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: The surplus after direct costs was $810,000 − $486,000 = $324,000 in 2024 and $900,000 − $495,000 = $405,000 in 2025. Operating return on sales used $81,000 ÷ $810,000 × 100 and $108,000 ÷ $900,000 × 100. Operating return on the capital base used $81,000 ÷ $540,000 × 100 and $108,000 ÷ $600,000 × 100. Revenue rose $90,000 while direct costs rose only $9,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The surplus share of sales rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, reflecting strong control of direct costs despite the 4.6% complaint rate. The operating share of sales rose from 10.0% to 12.0%, showing fixed costs were spread across more trips. Return on capital rose from 15.0% to 18.0% even though capital employed increased from $540,000 to $600,000, so the company is earning more from its larger asset base. Interest payable fell from $13,500 to $12,000, helping the outcome, but the 5.1% base rate may reverse that.

Conclusion: HLF's profitability has improved. The 40.0% to 45.0% surplus margin, 10.0% to 12.0% operating margin and 15.0% to 18.0% return on capital all confirm this. The strongest evidence is the rise in return on capital, because it shows the extra capital behind the $560,000 ferry is generating higher profit rather than the gain coming only from higher sales. The 8.5% fall in day-trip spending is a future risk rather than a 2025 result, so it does not alter this conclusion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified improved judgement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HLF of introducing a $1.20 guaranteed-seat premium fare.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 420 tourists found 70% would pay $1.20 more for a guaranteed-seat premium service, while 55% still book by price. Adding the premium to the $13.50 fare with the $8.00 variable cost unchanged lifts contribution from $5.50 toward $6.70, giving more cash for the $560,000 ferry, and offers price-sensitive tourists a clearer reason to book early.

Disadvantage: A guaranteed seat is hard to deliver while 4.6% of passengers complain, 3.4% of tickets are refunded and only 89% of sailings leave on time. Failed guarantees would create more complaints and refunds, but the insert gives no compensation cost, so the net gain cannot be calculated. Crew absenteeism and the 42-minute berth turnaround could also make the promise expensive to honour, especially with coastal day-trip spending down 8.5%. HLF should monitor the 26 written complaints before extending the guarantee to peak sailings.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HLF's survey, service record and cost data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.1%, the 2.1% rise in marine fuel and electricity prices and the 8.5% fall in coastal day-trip consumer spending will affect HLF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (4.4% to 5.1%): The increase is 0.7 percentage points. If the $320,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the added interest is 0.007 × $320,000 = $2,240 a year, small next to $220,000 of fixed costs and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. The main residual effect is a higher cost of any future finance for the $560,000 ferry programme, which HLF can limit by fixing the rate.

Marine fuel and electricity prices (up 2.1%): Only an upper bound is defensible because the insert gives one $8.00 variable cost without decomposition. If all of that $8.00 rose 2.1%, the added cost is 0.021 × $8.00 = $0.17 a trip, or about $10,080 a year at 60,000 trips (60,000 × $0.17), trimming contribution from $5.50 toward $5.33. The stated rise is small, so the effect is modest.

Coastal day-trip spending (down 8.5%): The insert does not link spending directly to HLF's volumes, so an illustrative bound is the honest approach. If trips fell in line with the 8.5% fall, that is 0.085 × 60,000 = 5,100 fewer trips, each carrying $5.50 of contribution, a $28,050 reduction. The 2.7% rise in city-break spending offers only a partial offset because HLF serves coastal routes.

Conclusion: The 8.5% fall in coastal day-trip spending will have the greatest impact. Its illustrative $28,050 contribution loss exceeds the $10,080 energy upper bound and the conditional $2,240 interest effect, and it directly threatens the 60,000 trips needed to cover fixed costs. HLF should defend demand through hotel partnerships and the $1.20 premium rather than focus on the smaller cost changes.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to HLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HLF's demand, costs or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes using derivations shown from insert figures, with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
